lines: Welcome to the CURTIS Digital Briefing. I'm Grant.
And I'm Maya. Today we're unpacking a paper from Carnegie Mellon and Google, published this October, called Spec-Driven Development as Prescribed and as Practiced.

If you lead product or engineering, and your teams are adopting AI coding agents, this is probably the most useful empirical study on the topic so far. Mostly because it's the first broad one that wasn't written by someone selling the tool.

Right. Quick framing. Spec-driven development, or SDD, means writing a specification, usually a Markdown file, before an agent implements anything. The agent reads the spec to plan, build, and verify. GitHub has Spec Kit, Amazon has Kiro, Fission AI has OpenSpec.
And it's spreading fast. The researchers found spec files in over seventy-three thousand public GitHub repos, almost all first committed in 2025 or later.
The vendor pitch is better quality, less agent drift, and higher productivity. The paper asks a simple question. What do people actually do, and how does it differ from what the tools prescribe?

Three sources. A thematic analysis of Reddit discussions. Interviews with twenty-one practitioners, eight of whom built SDD tools. And a sample of two hundred sixty-six active, popular repositories from a corpus they're releasing, called SpecMine, which holds about four hundred seventy thousand spec files.
The tool-maker versus tool-user split is the clever part. The makers' accounts match the documentation. So wherever users diverge from makers, that's practice departing from prescription.
One caveat to carry the whole way through. The repo sample is mostly OpenSpec and Spec Kit, about eighty-nine percent of files. And everything here is association, not causation.
